title: Avian influenza A(H5N1) human cases – United States – 2024-2026

analysis.time: The outbreak was first reported on 15 October 2026, with the latest update on 19 October 2026. The US CDC has been monitoring the situation since 1 April 2024, and the ECDC has been assessing the risk since 25 February 2025.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak has been reported in 13 states in the United States, including Washington, California, Colorado, Michigan, Nevada, Texas, Iowa, Ohio, Oregon, Wisconsin, Louisiana, Wyoming, and Missouri. The affected population includes dairy workers, poultry farm workers, and individuals with exposure to backyard flocks, wild birds, or other mammals.

Since 1 April 2024, 72 human cases have been reported, including one death, with no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: As of 15 October 2026, 72 human cases of avian influenza A(H5N1) have been reported in the US, with 42 cases linked to dairy cattle exposure and 24 to poultry farm outbreaks. Three cases involved exposure to other animals, and three had no known animal exposure. The US CDC states the risk to the general population remains low, but it is moderate to high for individuals with close or prolonged exposure to infected animals or contaminated environments.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Public health authorities have initiated contact tracing and symptom monitoring of close contacts. The US CDC and ECDC are collaborating to monitor the situation, with ECDC emphasizing the need for enhanced surveillance, testing of exposed individuals, and communication of the epidemiological situation. The risk assessment for the general population is considered low, while for those with occupational exposure, it is low-to-moderate.

The risk to the general population is low, but it is moderate to high for individuals with close contact to infected animals or contaminated environments. Public health authorities have implemented contact tracing, symptom monitoring, and testing of exposed individuals. The US CDC and ECDC are collaborating to monitor the situation and update risk assessments as new information emerges. The ECDC has noted that the genotype B3.13, found in US dairy cattle and human cases, has not been detected in Europe, and the risk for the EU/EEA remains low. Measures include providing guidance, testing symptomatic individuals, and ensuring access to personal protective equipment (PPE) for dairy workers.

title: Poultry-exposed people around Poyang Lake showed varied avian influenza antibody reactivity, 2018–2025 - Bioengineer.org

analysis.time: The study was conducted from 2018 to 2025, with samples collected annually during winter and spring. The publication date is October 20, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The study focused on poultry-exposed individuals in Nanchang County and Duchang and Wuning counties, Jiujiang, Jiangxi Province, China. It included 2,437 serum samples from backyard poultry keepers, their household members, and live poultry market workers.
analysis.event: A cross-sectional serological surveillance study found varied antibody reactivity to seven avian influenza virus subtypes among poultry-exposed people around Poyang Lake between 2018 and 2025. The results describe antibody reactivity, not clinically diagnosed infections.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Antibody reactivity was observed in 4.43% of samples for H5N6 and 4.39% for H9N2. For H7N9, 2.74% of samples met the threshold during 2018–2020, and 1.44% for H3N8 from 2021 through 2025. The study notes that these findings do not establish subtype-specific human infection or local circulation of the viruses.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study is an observational, cross-sectional survey, and the results are based on antibody reactivity. The National Influenza Center performed the assays, and the authors suggest continued serological surveillance alongside poultry and environmental virological data for risk assessment. The number of samples tested varied across subtypes, locations, and years, limiting direct comparisons.

analysis.brief_en: A cross-sectional serological study conducted between 2018 and 2025 around Poyang Lake, Jiangxi Province, China, found varied antibody reactivity to avian influenza virus subtypes among poultry-exposed individuals. The study included 2,437 serum samples from backyard poultry keepers, their household members, and live poultry market workers in Nanchang County and Duchang and Wuning counties. Antibody positivity was observed for H5N6 (4.43%), H9N2 (4.39%), H7N9 (2.74% from 2018–2020), and H3N8 (1.44% from 2021–2025). The findings do not confirm subtype-specific human infections or local circulation of the viruses. The National Influenza Center performed hemagglutination-inhibition assays, and the authors recommend continued surveillance combined with virological data for risk assessment. The study notes that sample numbers varied across subtypes, locations, and years, limiting direct comparisons. The results are based on antibody reactivity, not clinical diagnoses, and the article is presented in an accepted, citable version that may undergo further edits before publication.

title: H5N1 Avian Influenza Confirmed at Vandalur Zoo - GK Today

analysis.time: The outbreak was confirmed on 2 October 2026, with the first bird death reported on 3 October and no further deaths or illness signs reported since 9 October. The zoo closed to visitors on 22 and 23 October 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak occurred at Arignar Anna Zoological Park (Vandalur Zoo) in Chennai, Tamil Nadu, affecting water birds housed in the Vedanthangal enclosure.
analysis.event: H5N1 avian influenza was confirmed in water birds at Vandalur Zoo, reported by the National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (NIHSAD), Bhopal.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Seven water birds died between 3 and 9 October 2026. The outbreak is described as likely over by the zoo director. No human infections or broader community impact were reported.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The zoo implemented biosecurity measures, including disinfection, sanitisation, restricted access, and closure to visitors for two days. The National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases confirmed the infection, and the zoo director assessed the outbreak as likely over.

analysis.brief_en: H5N1 avian influenza was confirmed in water birds at Vandalur Zoo in Chennai, Tamil Nadu, on 2 October 2026, with seven birds dying between 3 and 9 October. The National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (NIHSAD) in Bhopal verified the infection. The zoo cordoned off the affected area and closed to visitors on 22 and 23 October to enforce biosecurity measures, including disinfection and restricted access. The zoo director noted the outbreak as likely over after no further deaths or illness signs were reported. No human infections or broader community impact were mentioned in the evidence. The affected birds were housed in the Vedanthangal enclosure, which included painted storks, grey pelicans, grey herons, and oriental darters. The outbreak highlights the need for vigilance in animal facilities regarding avian influenza transmission.

title: US records first human case of H5N1 this year

analysis.time: A man in Washington has tested positive for H5N1, marking the first human case of bird flu in the US this year.
analysis.location_and_population: Washington, United States; dairy farm workers.
analysis.event: The patient was reportedly infected after being exposed to two infected cows.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The strain circulating among US dairy cattle, clade 2.3.4.4b, has proven less lethal to humans. Since the virus first spilled over into American dairy cattle, there have been at least 72 human cases of H5N1 in the US, almost all of whom had close contact with sick animals. Two of those infected died. The person is not seriously ill and is isolating at home.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Washington health officials stated that the risk to the public remained "low" and "fits the pattern seen across the US dairy outbreak: infection through direct occupational contact with infected animals." Scientists have warned that if H5N1 mutates and gains the ability to spread person-to-person, it could trigger the next global pandemic.

analysis.brief_en: A man in Washington has tested positive for H5N1, marking the first human case of bird flu in the US this year. The patient, who works on a dairy farm, was reportedly infected after being exposed to two infected cows. H5N1 has become endemic on US dairy farms since 2024, with over 1,000 herds infected across dozens of states. The individual is not seriously ill and is isolating at home. Scientists warn that if H5N1 mutates to spread between humans, it could trigger a global pandemic. Washington health officials note the risk to the public remains low, as infections are primarily through direct contact with sick animals. The strain circulating among US dairy cattle, clade 2.3.4.4b, has been less lethal to humans compared to other strains. Since the virus first spilled over into American dairy cattle, there have been at least 72 human cases, with two deaths reported. The virus has also infected nearly 100 different animal species, including bears, lions, foxes, mink, dolphins, porpoises, dogs, and cats. However, the spread of H5N1 is primarily linked to poultry farms, where over 500 million birds have been culled since 2021. The situation highlights the need for vigilance and testing among high-risk populations, such as dairy farm workers, many of whom are undocumented and avoid testing programs due to fears of contact with law enforcement.

The report notes that HPAI has been circulating across the continent, with over 1,000 outbreaks reported in 10 countries. While the risk to the general population is considered low, the CDC announced a COCA Call for clinicians on the same day to address the spread of Dengue in the United States, particularly in Florida, where nearly 300 imported cases were recorded. The FAO emphasized the need for vigilance, especially in areas where wild birds congregate and poultry farms are located nearby. The report also mentions that standard influenza tests may not detect novel strains like H5N1, and that surveillance gaps persist due to resource limitations and political or economic factors. analysis.location_and_population: Multiple Indiana counties, specifically Hamilton County and Greene County, with wild waterfowl and raptors as the affected population. The report also mentions domestic and agricultural animals such as poultry, cattle, and cats as susceptible.
analysis.event: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) was confirmed as the cause of death for multiple geese in Hamilton County and multiple blue-wing teal in Greene County. The Indiana Department of Natural Resources and the U.S. Department of Agriculture Wildlife Services and DNR Division of Fish, Wildlife & Nature Preserves reported the findings.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The confirmed cases involve multiple geese and blue-wing teal. However, it is possible for humans to contract the disease, and the report emphasizes the need for caution.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The Indiana Department of Health is advised to contact if symptoms develop after handling sick or dead waterfowl. The public is instructed to avoid contact with sick wildlife, wear protective gear when handling carcasses, and report any suspicious cases. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention note that the public health risk for HPAI is low, but humans can contract the disease. The public is advised to avoid contact with sick or dead waterfowl and raptors, wear disposable gloves and a mask when handling carcasses, and report any suspicious cases to the Indiana Department of Health. Symptoms such as fever, cough, and diarrhea should be reported immediately. The report also highlights the susceptibility of domestic animals like poultry, cattle, and cats to HPAI and recommends biosecurity measures to prevent spread.
